notableFigures.name: Saren-Vel
notableFigures.title: The First Riven
notableFigures.backstory:
Before she was the first Riven, Saren-Vel was the most powerful Athien pact-caster of her generation, a contract-lawyer and arcanist whose binding-clauses were so precise that Morvane itself had never found a loophole in her work. She drafted the trade-treaty that opened Ironjaw Port to the Solari. She wrote the inheritance-contract that resolved a three-century dispute between two competing Athien bloodlines. She was, by any measure, the apotheosis of what a Athien could become.

And she was unraveling.

The records are incomplete, her personal ledger was among the documents consumed by the Severing flame, but the surviving testimony suggests she had been breaking small contracts for decades. A promise here, a receipt there, a ritual obligation skipped. Each breach felt like freedom. Each breach brought the Fading closer. By the time she walked into the bog, she was perhaps six months from dissolution, still functional, still brilliant, but slowly coming apart at the edges like a manuscript left in damp air.

The flame she carried was no ordinary fire. It had been prepared over thirty years, a slow extraction of pure annihilation, the inverse of the pact's preservation. It did not burn wood or flesh or paper. It burned *ink.* Specifically, it burned the ink that recorded her name in every active copy of the First Contract. When she touched the flame to the contract in Atropolis, her name vanished simultaneously from Ironjaw Port, from the Frostwood embassy, from every outpost and archive and personal ledger in the Athien trade network. The silence that followed lasted seventeen seconds. Every Athien alive at that moment counted them.

Saren-Vel did not disappear. She walked out of the First Contract Chamber, past the Athien guards who could not touch her because no contract authorized them to, through the streets of Atropolis where Athien stared at her with expressions that had no precedent, and into the deep bog where the Riven still gather. She has been seen periodically in the four centuries since, always at a distance, always silent, always watching something no one else can see. The Riven revere her as their founder. The Athien consider her the greatest legal crisis in Athien history, a person who exists outside the pact, and therefore outside the law, and therefore cannot be wrong about anything because "wrong" requires a standard she no longer acknowledges.

She has never spoken. No one knows if she still can.

notableFigures.name: Lyra-Vel
notableFigures.title: The Twelfth-Generation Oracle
notableFigures.backstory:
The Oracle of Atropolis is not a title. It is a person, always a Athien, always female, always the eldest living Athien who has returned more times than any other. Lyra-Vel is the twelfth to hold the position. She has returned fourteen times: four illnesses, three accidents, five acts of violence, and two causes she refuses to disclose. Her death-count is the highest in recorded Athien history, and Morvane knows her voice.

Lyra-Vel does not read the future. She reads the First Contract, not the text, but the implications. She perceives the contract-graph the way Weft perceive the obligation-web, but deeper, older, more structural. When a new contract is signed anywhere in the Athien trade network, she feels the shift in the pact's balance. When a contract is broken, she knows before the Vezan rises. When Morvane's attention wavers, as it has been doing, increasingly, in the last century, she is the first to notice.

The Athien consult her before every major policy decision. She never tells them what to do. She tells them what the pact allows, what the pact forbids, and what the pact has never been asked before, and lets them draw their own conclusions. The youngest Athien find her terrifying. The oldest Athien find her comforting. Lyra-Vel herself finds both reactions mildly disappointing.

She has been writing a personal addendum to the First Contract for two hundred years, a document that no one else has been permitted to read. Some believe it is a record of every return, every threshold, every conversation with Morvane. Others believe it is a legal argument for the pact's dissolution, a case she is building so slowly that no one alive will see it filed. Lyra-Vel has never clarified. When asked, she says only: "Morvane has not asked me to stop writing."

notableFigures.name: Orven-Sen
notableFigures.title: The Gambler Who Bet on the Sun
notableFigures.backstory:
The most famous Weft in Athien history made only one bet that anyone remembers, and he made it sixty-three years before Emberspire erupted.

Orven-Sen was a mid-level probability-weaver attached to the Ironjaw Port trade delegation, competent, unremarkable, never promoted. His specialty was predicting shipping outcomes: which routes would ice over, which caravans would be delayed, which trade agreements would default. He was accurate enough to be employed and not accurate enough to be feared.

In the spring of the year that would later be known as the Year of the First Ash, Orven-Sen walked into the Ironjaw Port contract-hall and filed a formal prediction with the trade-registry: the volcano Emberspire, dormant since the pre-Binding era, would erupt within a century. Its eruption would shatter the Sundale surface and create a new thermal equilibrium. The Athien should immediately renegotiate all warmth-resource contracts with the Solari forge-clans to include eruption-contingency clauses.

The contract-hall laughed. Emberspire was a dead mountain. The Solari themselves believed the sun slept beneath it, but no one, not even the Solari, expected it to wake.

Orven-Sen was not laughed out of the hall. He was fined for filing a frivolous prediction. He paid the fine. He returned to his desk. He continued predicting shipping outcomes for another forty years, never mentioning Emberspire again, and died of a blood-contract complication (a clause he had signed at nineteen that came due at seventy-two, as he had always known it would) without ever seeing his prediction come true.

Sixty-three years after his death, Emberspire erupted. The Athien trade-registry discovered, in the chaos of renegotiation, that the contingency clauses Orven-Sen had quietly inserted into three generations of warmth-resource contracts, clauses no one had noticed because no one read the fine print of a fined gambler's filing, were still legally active. The Athien saved an estimated four million gold-weight in renegotiation costs because a dead Weft had been right sixty-three years ahead of schedule and had the patience to wait.

No one knows what he bet. No one knows what broke when he tugged that thread. Somewhere in the Gloom, a tree died. Somewhere in the Iceheart Sea, a ship went down. Somewhere in the Frostwood Reach, a promise was broken that should have been kept. Orven-Sen never knew, and if he had, he would have considered it a fair price.

notableFigures.name: Vaelis the Scribe
notableFigures.title: The One Who Drafted the First Contract
notableFigures.backstory:
Vaelis was the eldest of the dying clan of scribes who walked into the deep wood and presented Morvane with an argument. She was eighty-three years old when the first freeze reached the Gloom. She had outlived two husbands, three children, and an entire legal tradition that died when the sun was stolen and the trade routes collapsed. She had been writing contracts for sixty-one years. She had never lost a case.

The argument she drafted was three pages long. She wrote it in three hours while her youngest grandchild, a girl named Thira, seven years old, already silver-mottled with frostbite, slept in her lap. The argument was not a prayer. It was not a supplication. It was a legal brief addressed to an entity with no known jurisdiction, citing precedents from a civilization that no longer existed, demanding terms that had never been negotiated before.

When Morvane accepted, when the silver bloomed across Vaelis's skin and her breath stopped in her chest, she did not weep. She did not celebrate. She looked at her granddaughter, whose frostbite had vanished, whose skin now shimmered with the same pure-silver luminescence, whose dark eyes reflected the canopy-light like a mirror, and she said: *"The terms are binding. We must begin the archive."*

Vaelis lived for another one hundred and forty-seven years. She personally wrote the first three thousand contracts in the Atropolis archive. She established the formatting conventions that the Athien still use, clause numbering, witness requirements, enforcement mechanisms. She refused to take a title. She refused to be called the founder. She insisted, until her final return, that she had simply been the scribe on duty when the argument needed to be written.

She returned twice: once from the wasting-disease that had killed her first husband (she had caught it from him, decades later, through a preserved letter that still carried the contagion), and once from an assassination attempt by a human trade delegation that had realized, too late, what they had signed. The second return took something from her, she never specified what, but her handwriting changed afterward, and she stopped writing contracts about love.

Her original draft of the First Contract is preserved in the deepest chamber of Atropolis, visible through living heartwood that has grown around it for centuries beyond counting. The ink has faded. The text is barely legible. But the tree that holds it is still alive, and the roots that anchor it reach all the way down to Morvane's threshold, and somewhere in those roots the original argument still vibrates, a question asked once, answered forever.

majorLocations.name: Atropolis
majorLocations.description:
The heart of Athien civilization and the largest living structure in the Bryngloom Forest. Atropolis is not a city of stone. It is a cultivated cathedral-grove, the oldest ironwood trees in the Gloom, each one shaped over a thousand years into cathedral-spaces where the Athien live, work, and archive. The trees are still growing. The oldest chambers, deep in the heartwood, date to the first generation after Morvane's bargain. The newest, in the outer canopy, are still being coaxed into shape by Athien wood-speakers who have been guiding the same branch for eighty years.

Walkways of living branch and bioluminescent moss connect the tree-structures at every level. At night the city glows faintly with the same cold light that runs through Athien veins, not bright, not warm, but steady, eternal, the color of moonlight on still water. The streets are named after signatories of the First Contract. The buildings are named after the contracts they house.

The deepest chamber of the oldest tree, the Heart-Vault, contains the First Contract itself, visible through living heartwood that has grown around the original document over centuries beyond counting. The text is barely legible now, but the tree remembers it. The roots remember it. Morvane remembers it. Athien make pilgrimage to the Heart-Vault at least once in their lives to press their tendrils against the bark and feel the original argument vibrating beneath, a question asked once, answered forever.

majorLocations.name: Ironjaw Port
majorLocations.description:
The Athien's largest external outpost, built into the frozen cliffs of the Iceheart Sea where the Bryngloom Forest meets the churning, freezing waves. The port is a wonder of Athien engineering: a series of living ironwood platforms coaxed from a cliff-face over three centuries, connected by branch-bridges and suspended trade galleries that sway gently in the perpetual sea-winds. Below the platforms, the Athien have cultivated buoyant fungal-rafts that serve as docks, the only structures in the known world that can withstand the Iceheart's storm-cycle without shattering.

Ironjaw is the Athien's economic lung. Every trade route between the Gloom and the outside world passes through it, Solari thermal salts, Myrathil foam-glass, human lumber, Mimir mask-repair materials, Mycellan fungal-light exports. The port houses a copy of the First Contract, which means Athien stationed here do not Fade. The copy is weaker than the Atropolis original, the Archive-Tether reaches about half as far from Ironjaw, which limits how far Athien trade-ships can sail before they must turn back.

The port is run by a mixed Athien-Weft council that has been quietly feuding for two hundred years over tariff policy. The human dock-workers who handle the physical labor are indentured to the port through inherited contracts their great-grandparents signed during the first freeze. The terms are fair, the Athien insist on fair terms, but the terms are also eternal, and the workers' grandchildren will inherit the same debt their ancestors accepted.

majorLocations.name: The Severing Bog
majorLocations.description:
The deepest part of the Bryngloom Forest, where the canopy thins and the preserving bog takes over. The mycelial network is sparse here, the fungal threads that sustain Athien life cannot penetrate the bog's chemical depths, and the pact's authority is correspondingly weak. This is where Saren-Vel walked to burn her name from the First Contract, and it is where every Severing has been performed since.

The bog is a sacred and terrifying place to the Athien. The Athien refuse to enter it, not out of prohibition, but because the thinning pact-authority makes them feel physically ill, like a limb going numb, like forgetting a word they have used their whole life. The Weft visit occasionally, to read the probability-web at its sparsest point and see what patterns emerge in the silence. The Riven live here, or near here, small camps of the severed, sustained by foraging and hunting rather than the pact, trading with each other in a gift-economy that would appall any Athien who witnessed it.

The exact spot where Saren-Vel performed the first Severing is unmarked. No one who has found it has ever described it. The Riven who perform Severings here say that the flame must be prepared over at least a decade, extraction of pure annihilation, the inverse of the pact's preservation, and that the process is excruciating in a way that has nothing to do with pain. The name burns. The silence that follows is the first true silence the Athien has felt since birth. Most Riven describe it as relief. A few describe it as grief.

majorLocations.name: The Canopy-Ledger
majorLocations.description:
Not a single location but a network, the living archive that connects every Athien settlement to every other. The Canopy-Ledger is the mycelial memory of the Athien civilization: every contract ever signed, stored in memory-glass tablets that grow from crystallized tree-sap and release their contents directly into the reader's mind when touched. The tablets are alive, requiring periodic exposure to the forest's bioluminescence to recharge their stored light.

The Ledger extends across the full reach of the Athien trade network, Atropolis, Ironjaw Port, the Frostwood embassy, the Sundale crossroads, with each outpost maintaining its own localized archive that synchronizes with the main Canopy-Ledger whenever a Athien courier travels between them. The synchronization is never perfect; there is always a lag, always a gap, always a contract that was signed in Ironjaw and won't reach Atropolis for another month. The Athien find this administrative imperfection maddening. The Weft find it useful, a gap in the record is a gap in the obligation-web, and gaps can be exploited.

The oldest tablets in the Ledger date to the first generation after the pact, the first three thousand contracts written by Vaelis the Scribe herself. They still glow, faintly. The memory-glass resists decay the same way the pact resists death: slowly, imperfectly, but so far, inexhaustibly.

neth.currentCrisis:
Three things are troubling the Athien, and none of them have been spoken aloud in the contract-halls of Atropolis.

The first is Morvane's attention. The elders who have returned many times, the ones whose death-count exceeds ten, who have stood at the threshold often enough to know Morvane's presence by its weight, report that something has changed. Morvane is distant. Colder. Absent for longer periods, as if something else has its attention, something larger, something elsewhere, something that is making the preservation of one forest-boundary entity and its contract-bound partners seem like a smaller priority than it used to be. The younger Athien cannot feel this. They have nothing to compare it to. But the elders are afraid, and the elders do not frighten easily.

The second is the Unraveling. The number of Athien who have begun the Unraveling, breaking contracts in sequence, feeling the temporary freedom, inching toward dissolution, has tripled in the last fifty years. No one has published the statistics. The statistics exist; the Weft can read them in the obligation-web, and the Athien can find them in the Canopy-Ledger if they look. The cause is unclear. Some blame Morvane's distraction, a weaker pact is easier to break. Some blame the cultural stagnation, the young are rebelling because the old have been frozen for centuries and show no sign of thawing. Some blame the Severing itself, every name burned from the First Contract weakens the pact slightly, and there have been more Severings in the last century than in the three centuries before.

The third is the bloodline-fracture. The three subraces have always existed in tension, but that tension has been functional for centuries beyond counting. Now it is becoming something else. The Athien are consolidating power, they control the contract-halls, the trade delegations, the external diplomacy. The Weft are withdrawing, fewer of them attend the contract-halls, fewer of them submit their probability-predictions for official record. The Riven are multiplying, the Severing is becoming less rare, less stigmatized, more visible, and the Athien have no legal mechanism to stop it because the Severing is not illegal. It simply removes the severer from legal existence, which makes prosecution impossible.

Somewhere in the deep bog, a Riven elder, perhaps Saren-Vel herself, perhaps someone who has never spoken their name aloud, is preparing an argument. No one knows what it argues. No one knows to whom it is addressed. But the Weft can feel it in the obligation-web: a new clause forming, a new contract being drafted, a new case being prepared. And the defendant has not yet been named.
neth.culturalPractices:
Every Athien child learns to read before they learn to speak. The first object placed in a newborn's hands is a memory-glass tablet, blank, uninscribed, waiting. The child is expected to feel the glass respond to their touch, to understand that information lives in light and light lives in the trees, to know before they can articulate it that their species is defined by the contract between memory and preservation.

The Stillness is the Athien's most intimate ritual. Four hours of trance, eyes open, body motionless, mind adrift in Morvane's archive. During the Stillness, the Athien does not sleep, they *listen.* They hear the mycelial network's slow pulse, the contract-clauses being written and fulfilled and broken across the trade network, the distant presence of Morvane at the threshold. A Athien emerging from Stillness is refreshed but also haunted, they have spent four hours in the presence of everything their species has promised, and some of those promises are heavier than others.

The Annual Renegotiation is the Athien calendar's central event. On the anniversary of the First Contract's signing, every active Athien contract within a given jurisdiction is reviewed for continued validity. Clauses that have expired are struck. Clauses that remain relevant are renewed. Clauses that no longer serve their original purpose are renegotiated, this is the only time of year when contract terms can be altered without penalty. The Renegotiation is a festival, a legal proceeding, and a religious observance simultaneously. Young Athien test the edges of their binding. Old Athien reassert the terms of their power. And somewhere, at the threshold, Morvane listens to the collective sound of its partners adjusting their agreements.

Athien do not bury their dead. They do not burn them. When a Athien's physical form finally fails beyond even the pact's preservation, when the body has been returned too many times, when Morvane declines to renegotiate the terms, the body is carried to the Heart-Vault in Atropolis and placed against the living heartwood that encases the First Contract. Over months, the tree absorbs the body, the pale skin softens into bark, the dark eyes become knots in the wood, the hair dissolves into root-thread. The Athien becomes part of the tree that holds the contract that preserved them. The oldest trees in Atropolis are the oldest Athien who ever lived, and if you press your palm against the bark in the right place, you can still feel the memory-glass pulse of contracts they signed before the sun was buried.

The Athien do not love Morvane. They respect it the way a debtor respects a creditor who has been patient for age upon age. When a Athien returns from the threshold, pulled back from a near-death by the pact's preservation, they do not thank Morvane. They renegotiate their terms. A returned Athien owes a new clause in their life-contract: a restriction, an obligation, a promise they did not make but now must keep. The deaths are not gifts. They are loans, and the interest compounds.

birthrightQuestions.description: At character creation, answer: how many times have you returned, and what did the last return take from you? The answer is purely narrative, no mechanics, but it defines your character's relationship to the pact, Morvane, and their own mortality.

prompts.name: Returned Once
prompts.question: You were young. A childhood fever that should have killed you, or a fall that should have shattered you, or a blade that slipped. Morvane's presence at the threshold was your first experience of anything beyond your own body, a vast, patient, utterly alien attention that considered you for a long moment and then said (not in words, not in language, but in the sudden absence of cold): *not yet.* You barely remember it. You have spent the rest of your life wondering if it really happened, if Morvane is real, if the pact is anything more than a story the elders tell to make their immortality bearable. The other Athien pity your innocence. They also envy it.

prompts.name: Returned Three Times
prompts.question: You have crossed the threshold three times: illness, accident, violence. Morvane knows your presence now. The last return took a memory, not the memory of the death itself (those never fade), but a memory from *before.* Morvane asked for something as payment for the renegotiation: a face, a name, a moment of warmth. You gave it. You do not remember what it was. The absence is a dull ache, like a tooth that was pulled and replaced with nothing. Sometimes, in Stillness, you feel the shape of what you lost pressing against the gap, recognizable, familiar, almost recoverable, and then the trance ends and the shape dissolves and you are left with the ache alone. The other Athien respect your experience. They also fear it.

prompts.name: Returned Seven Times
prompts.question: Seven returns. Morvane says your name now, or something that functions as a name in the space between language and silence where the renegotiations happen. The last return took something you did not want to give: a promise, a person, a piece of your future. The terms were clear. You accepted them because the alternative was the silence that waits for those who break the pact entirely. You do not speak of what you gave. You do not speak of who you gave it to. But sometimes, in crowded rooms, you catch yourself looking for someone you know is not there, someone whose absence is a clause in your life-contract that you read every morning and still, somehow, do not understand. The other Athien are afraid of you. You are afraid of what you will give next time.

prompts.name: Never Returned
prompts.question: You have never crossed the threshold. You are young, perhaps only thirty or forty, barely an adult by Athien standards, or you have been impossibly lucky, or you have been impossibly careful. You live in quiet dread of the first return. Every other Athien you know has crossed and come back different. What if you do not come back at all? What if you come back wrong, colder, harder, something Morvane touched too firmly and left a mark on? The other Athien treat you with a strange mixture of protectiveness and distance, as if you are not yet fully one of them, as if the first return is the real birth, and you are still waiting to be born. They are not wrong.

velun.name: Nethien
velun.illustrationCaption: “In Atropolis, every breath is notarized and every promise is recorded in sovereign ink. The law outlives the flesh.” — High Magistrate Vael

illustrations.caption: Atropolis & The Great Ledger Chancery — Sovereign marble law-metropolis and legal archive of the Athien.
Chancery-Gate Customs Port & Toll Arch — Fortified maritime harbor basin where foreign galleons are surveyed and assessed for sovereign tariffs.
The Great Balance Mint & Bedrock Vaults — Subterranean bedrock treasury and water-driven coin press beneath Atropolis.
Athien Contract-Magistrate — Aristocratic bust of an immortal pact-lord with obsidian-black eyes, silver-white hair, and ghost-silk court mantle.
Lady Sovereign Aurelia-Sen — Chief Comptroller of the Sovereign Mint holding delicate gold assay balances and an iron-bound credit ledger.
Ledger-Inquisitor Lucian — Contract-enforcement bailiff and auditor of blood debts with arrest warrant roll and rapier.
Moneyer Titus — Master coin engraver and mint die-cutter shaping imperial gold planchets at his anvil.

velun.visualDescription: The inheritors of Morvane's authority carry the pact in their bearing. Like all Athien they are tall and slender, pale to the point of luminousness, with dark pool-like eyes, but a Athien's eyes are often described as reflecting a contract-glyph spiraling slowly around the pupil that only they can see. Their colorless spider-silk hair is worn long under layered ghost-silk robes of pale, authoritative cut. Their chests do not visibly rise and fall with breath, the stilled mark of the pact made visible, and they move with the unhurried certainty of people whose every word may be enforced by a god.
velun.tooltipSummary: Contract-lords whose words carry binding weight, commanding authority through the Pact's enforceable legacy.
velun.description: The original pact-bound Athien bloodline, predating later Riven severance. They cannot knowingly make false pact-enforced assertions; withholding, conditional statements and literal loopholes are distinct. Morvane enforces actual First Contract obligations, not every unrelated patron's bargain or every hypothetical statement. Their preserved bodies and spoken clauses carry the partnership's authority within its scope.
velun.culturalBackground:
The Athien trace their bloodline to the original scribes who presented the First Contract to Morvane, Vaelis the Scribe's direct descendants, generation by generation, clause by clause. They run Atropolis. They write the contracts that govern Athien society. They negotiate with the Solari, the humans, the Mimir, anyone who needs Athien preservation-craft or Athien memory-glass, and their negotiations are always, always binding.

Athien children are educated in the contract-halls from the moment their pale skin stabilizes, usually around age five or six. They learn to read ancient scrolls and contract covenants before they learn to read spoken faces. They learn contract law before they learn ethics. They learn that every word they speak carries weight, and that weight accumulates, a careless promise at ten becomes a binding obligation at fifty, and Morvane does not distinguish between a child's protestation and an adult's oath.

A Athien's power is their voice. When they invoke a clause aloud, a binding, a sealing, a cosmic enforcement, the pact responds. The air thickens. The light shifts. Everyone in the room feels Morvane's attention settle on the proceedings like a held breath. A Athien who has perfected their craft can seal a contract with a single spoken sentence that no signatory can ever break, not without consequences that ripple across generations.

The flaw is inseparable from the gift: a knowingly false pact-enforced assertion is forbidden, and an actual obligation carries consequences. Withholding, literal loopholes, and conditional statements require careful wording but are not automatically new obligations. First Contract jurisdiction is bounded; it does not turn every child's protest or hypothetical into an omniscient universal contract.

They view the Weft with a mixture of admiration and unease, the Weft see the web behind the text, the implications the Athien cannot perceive, and that makes them useful and unpredictable. They view the Riven with something closer to horror, the Riven are what happens when a Athien decides the pact's weight is heavier than the silence, and the Athien cannot process a choice that results in legal non-existence.

traits.name: Bound Tongue
traits.description: Advantage on Persuasion when negotiating formal agreements. Knowingly false pact-enforced assertions are forbidden. Breaking an actual First Contract commitment deals the recorded 1d4 wyrd damage and Deception penalty; hypothetical statements, withholding and unrelated bargains are not automatically enforceable clauses.

effects.name: Morvane's Voice
effects.description: Advantage on Persuasion checks when making a formal agreement or negotiating contract terms. The pact echoes behind your words, the person across the table can feel the weight of the entity that enforces what you negotiate.
effects.mechanicsText: You have advantage on Persuasion checks when negotiating contract terms or entering formal agreements.

effects.name: The Bound Commitment
effects.description: Knowingly false pact-enforced assertions are forbidden. Deception checks about existing First Contract commitments are disadvantaged, and breaking an actual commitment deals 1d4 wyrd damage. Conditional statements and unrelated bargains are not automatically obligations.

statusEffect.description: First Contract scope only: no knowingly false enforced assertions; contractual Deception disadvantage and 1d4 wyrd on a broken actual commitment.

effects.mechanicsText: Bounded First Contract commitments only: contractual Deception disadvantage and the recorded 1d4 wyrd breach damage. Use the single Fraying track; no hypothetical-statement trap or universal patron jurisdiction.

traits.name: Clause of Binding
traits.description: Invoke Morvane's authority to seal a spoken agreement with pact-magic. The target who accepts your terms is cosmically bound: if they break the promise, Morvane exacts a price. But the clause binds you equally, if you break your own word, the price is yours to pay.

effects.name: Sealed by Morvane
effects.description: Speak a single, clear promise to a willing creature within 30 feet. For 24 hours, if they knowingly break the promise, they suffer 2d6 wyrd damage and disadvantage on their next d20 roll, Morvane enforces. The promise must be specific and achievable ("you will not harm my allies in this battle," not "you will be a good person").

effects.name: The Binder Bound
effects.description: If you yourself break the sealed promise, you suffer the same penalty, 2d6 wyrd damage and disadvantage on your next d20 roll. Morvane does not distinguish between signatories. A contract binds all parties equally.

statusEffect.description: Breaking your own sealed promise deals 2d6 psychic and imposes disadvantage on next d20 roll.

effects.mechanicsText: If you break a promise you sealed with Clause of Binding, you suffer the same penalty as the target: 2d6 wyrd damage and disadvantage on your next d20 roll.

traits.name: Canopy-Scholar
traits.description: +2 to History and Arcana checks involving the Bryngloom Forest, contract law, Morvane, Athien genealogy, or the Wyrd. Requires 1 hour of archive maintenance per long rest to keep the bonus; missing it forfeits the bonus until you spend 1+ hour catching up. (You trained in the Canopy-Ledger, the living archive where Athien contracts sit in crystallized tree-sap that pours knowledge straight into the reader's mind; your education never truly ended.)

effects.name: Ledger-Trained
effects.description: +2 to History and Arcana checks related to the Bryngloom Forest, contract law, Morvane, Athien genealogy, or the Wyrd. You have spent decades reading memory-glass in the canopy, the archive is not a place you visit. It is where you live.
effects.mechanicsText: You gain +2 to History and Arcana checks involving the Bryngloom Forest, contract law, Morvane, Athien genealogy, or the Wyrd.

effects.name: The Unfiled Record
effects.description: You must spend 1 hour per long rest maintaining your personal archive-record, reviewing contracts, updating genealogies, filing new observations in memory-glass. If you miss this maintenance, lose the Canopy-Scholar bonus until you spend 1 hour catching up. Two missed days = the bonus remains lost for 2 hours after resuming.

statusEffect.description: Lose Canopy-Scholar bonus after 24 hours without maintenance. Recover by spending 1+ hours updating records.

effects.mechanicsText: If you miss 1 hour of archive maintenance per long rest, you lose the Canopy-Scholar bonus until you spend 1+ hours catching up.

traits.name: Pact-Flame
traits.description: Once per long rest, invoke Morvane's authority against a target within 30 feet that has broken a promise, contract, or oath within the last 24 hours. The target takes 2d6 wyrd damage (no save). Morvane does not forgive debts, and your voice carries its collection notice.

effects.name: The Collector's Flame
effects.description: Target a creature within 30 feet that has broken a promise, contract, or oath within the last 24 hours. The target takes 2d6 wyrd damage with no saving throw. Morvane does not forgive debts.

statusEffect.description: 2d6 wyrd damage to an oath-breaker within 30 feet. No save.

effects.mechanicsText: Once per long rest, target a creature within 30 feet that broke a promise, contract, or oath in the last 24 hours, dealing 2d6 wyrd damage with no saving throw.

kessen.name: Weft
kessen.illustrationCaption: “Beneath the grand chanceries lies the Under-Ledger, where debts are settled in dark water and whisper-coin.” — Shadow-Canal Proverb

illustrations.caption: Under-Ledger Shadow-Exchange & Canals — Sovereign subterranean canal city and black-market haven of the Weft Athien.
Pawn-Wharf Basin & Sump Wharves — Sunken subterranean barter wharf on barnacle-encrusted timber stilts over an underground tidal lake.
Weft Shadow-Broker Portrait — Sly under-fog broker with slate-tinted skin, luminous coin-silver eyes, dark charcoal hair, and folding balance scale.
“The dice may tumble where they will, but the ledger always knows whose palm will scoop the winnings.” — Orven-Sen
Lyra-Vel — Blind subterranean oracle and water diviner creating concentric ripple prophecies in a ceramic canal scrying bowl.
Fence Vanya the Key-Caster — Master locksmith and relic appraiser inspecting a skeleton key with lockpicks and iron key rings.
Black-Ledger Broker Silas — Master information broker studying an iron-bound cipher ledger beside a hooded dark-lantern.
Night-Drifter Corin — Fearless subterranean canal sentry and smuggler boatman standing on the prow of his narrow skiff with poling-spear and lantern.

kessen.visualDescription: Sly, cunning, and razor-sharp, the Weft are the street-smart shadow-brokers of the Athien. Adapted to subterranean gloom and canal fog, they possess a lean, wiry silhouette with slate-tinted pale skin and dark charcoal-streaked black hair tied back loosely. Their most striking feature is their luminous coin-silver eyes, which reflect lantern-light like a cat's in the dark and dart with calculating intelligence. They dress in dark wool traveling capes with concealed pockets, waxed oilskin vests, fingerless gloves, and soft leather boots, carrying handheld brass balance scales, spring-loaded stilettos, and hooded dark-lanterns.
kessen.tooltipSummary: Sly and cunning under-fog shadow-brokers who exploit obligation-webs, trading contraband, secrets, and probability in subterranean canals.
kessen.description: The sly and cunning underworld subrace of the Athien. Operating in the misty subterranean canals and shadowed vaults beneath Atropolis, the Weft perceive the invisible obligation-threads of the world and exploit them with ruthless ingenuity. Rather than serving the rigid letter of the First Contract, they weave through its loopholes, trading in contraband debts, secret pledges, forged passes, and probability itself.
kessen.culturalBackground: Under-Ledger is the lower canal/undercity district among Atropolis's grown ironwood root works. Weft brokers, appraisers, couriers, and information merchants read obligation-threads and negotiate loopholes; criminal syndicates are particular institutions, not every person's morality. Their coin-silver eyes and pale frames carry the history of raw Well over-drawing. They remain pact-bound, with preservation and Fraying obligations distinct from the House's separate credit.

traits.name: Morvane's Sight
traits.description: Advantage on Insight checks to detect deception, read a creature's true loyalties, or gauge whether a promise is sincere. In social situations of more than 10 people you suffer disadvantage on Spirit and Charisma checks as the obligation-web overwhelms you, and your obligation-threads remain visible to any creature with supernatural perception. (You perceive the debt-threads binding all things; the web reveals everything, and the web is everywhere.)

effects.name: The Obligation-Web
effects.description: Advantage on Insight checks made to detect deception, determine a creature's true loyalties, or identify whether a promise is sincerely intended. You see the threads connecting speakers to their obligations, a lie is a broken thread, a sincere promise is a bright one.
effects.mechanicsText: You have advantage on Insight checks made to detect deception or assess a creature's true loyalties.

effects.name: Thread-Blindness
effects.description: In any social situation involving more than 10 people, crowded markets, court proceedings, battle councils, the obligation-web becomes overwhelming. Disadvantage on Spirit and Charisma checks as the threads of every promise, debt, and potential future clause compete for your attention. You see too much to focus on any one thing.
effects.mechanicsText: In social situations of more than 10 people, you have disadvantage on Spirit and Charisma checks as the overwhelming obligation-web fragments your focus.

effects.name: The Thread That Shows
effects.description: Other creatures with supernatural perception, other Weft, certain Wyrd-creatures, Morvane itself, can see the threads connecting you to your obligations. Your loyalties, your debts, your broken promises are visible in the web to anyone who knows how to look.

statusEffect.description: Obligation-threads visible to supernatural perception. Your debts and loyalties can be read.

effects.mechanicsText: Creatures with supernatural perception can see the obligation-threads connecting you to your debts and loyalties, reading them like an open ledger.

traits.name: Probability-Weave
traits.description: Tug a thread in the obligation-web at the precise moment. The universe rearranges itself around your intervention. Something elsewhere in the web snaps, you feel it break, but you will never know what it was.

effects.name: The Right Thread
effects.description: Once per short rest, when a creature within 60 feet makes an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw, you may use your reaction to grant them advantage or impose disadvantage on that roll. You are tugging the probability-thread at the critical moment, the shot hits, the persuasion lands, the save succeeds, or the reverse. The universe adjusts.

effects.name: The Snapped Thread
effects.description: When you use Probability-Weave, the GM secretly records a "snapped thread." At a future moment, within the same session, something unlucky happens to an NPC, a piece of the environment, or a distant event. A stranger's luck sours. A deal collapses. A message never arrives. You never know what broke, but you felt it break. The GM will tell you when you sense the snap, the location, never the consequence.

statusEffect.description: Each use of Probability-Weave snaps a thread elsewhere in the world. Consequences manifest at the GM's discretion.

effects.mechanicsText: Each use of Probability-Weave secretly snaps a thread elsewhere in the world, producing an unlucky event for an NPC, the environment, or a distant event at the GM's discretion.

traits.name: Temporal Ledger
traits.description: +2 to initiative rolls, and once per long rest you may ask the GM one truthful but cryptic question about the approaching consequences of a situation. A failed or ominous divination answer imposes disadvantage on your next initiative roll. (Time is the longest obligation-thread; you feel promises coming due long before they arrive.)

effects.name: The Approaching Due-Date
effects.description: +2 to initiative rolls. You can feel the imminence of events before they arrive, the weight of a consequence about to land, the tension of a promise about to be called in. and, once per long rest, you may ask the GM one question about the approaching consequences of a current situation: "What is about to catch up with us?" The GM gives a truthful but cryptic answer based on what the obligation-web reveals.
effects.mechanicsText: You gain +2 to initiative rolls and may ask the GM one truthful but cryptic question about approaching consequences once per long rest.

effects.name: Paralysis of Foresight
effects.description: When you fail the Temporal Ledger divination (ask a question and receive an unclear or ominous answer), you suffer disadvantage on your next initiative roll as the weight of approaching consequences clouds your reactions. You know something is coming. You cannot tell what.

statusEffect.description: Disadvantage on next initiative roll after a failed or ominous Temporal Ledger divination.

effects.mechanicsText: After a failed or ominous Temporal Ledger divination, you suffer disadvantage on your next initiative roll as the weight of approaching consequences clouds your reactions.

traits.name: Thread-Snap
traits.description: Once per long rest, when a creature within 60 feet makes an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw, you can force them to reroll and take the new result. You take 1d4 wyrd damage as the obligation-web recoils through your consciousness.

effects.name: The Severed Thread
effects.description: When a creature within 60 feet makes an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw, force them to reroll the d20 and take the new result. You choose after seeing the original roll. Once per long rest.

effects.name: The Recoil
effects.description: When you use Thread-Snap, you take 1d4 wyrd damage as the obligation-web recoils through your consciousness. You felt the thread snap, and it snapped through you.

statusEffect.description: Take 1d4 wyrd damage on use. The web recoils through the weaver.

effects.mechanicsText: When you use Thread-Snap, you take 1d4 wyrd damage as the obligation-web recoils through your consciousness.

drun.name: Riven

baseTraits.build: Gaunt, pale-skinned, breathing mortals with haunted pale-grey eyes

drun.illustrationCaption: “Among the ruins of Severance Hold, the Riven seek the silence that exists beyond all contracts.” — Chronicler of the Severed

illustrations.caption: Cinder-Grave & Severance Hold — Sovereign subterranean necropolis city of the Riven among pre-Calamity monastery ruins and cracked gothic arches.
The Inscription Catacombs & Vault of Lost Sins — Vaulted underground archive where epigraphers take charcoal rubbings of ancient monolithic stone steles.
The Arcane Kiln & Enchanting Sinks — Subterranean runic foundry and workshop where enchanters forge warding instruments and chisel reversal glyphs.
“Trace the broken glyphs until the penance is complete; even the severed soul may yet find equilibrium.” — Saren-Vel, First Riven

drun.visualDescription: Gaunt and haunting, the Riven bear the unpreserved pale frame of their kin, with paper-white dry skin, faint bluish veins, and pale-grey eyes in hollow sockets. Their chests rise and fall with ordinary breath. Wispy snow-white hair, rune-etched scars, ash-grey wraps, scholar bandoliers, stone-chisels, and severed debt-collars mark some ruin-scrivener traditions. Their souls were not universally stolen: the pact no longer preserves their bodies, and their appearance is not proof of undeath or ancestral guilt.
drun.tooltipSummary: Riven, finite-lived Athien who eat, drink, sleep, and build lives beyond the First Contract; ruin-scriveners are one of their traditions.
drun.description: The Riven descend from deliberate Severing, pioneered by Saren-Vel after the First Contract's founding. Burning their signatures from the pact removes its preservation and enforcement. They eat, drink, sleep, and slowly age. Pact authorities call this ancestral sin; it is not author truth that their souls were stolen. Their removed signatures defeat First Contract-keyed detection, not ordinary sight or every magical sensor.
drun.culturalBackground: Riven communities include ruin-scriveners, epigraphers, enchanters, couriers, and outcasts. Severance Hold preserves fallen libraries and underground workshops; Over-Shanty and Deep-Quarter serve other lives beyond pact administration. Scholars take rubbings and study salvaged relics for knowledge, restoration, or chosen craft, not a universal obligation to recover stolen souls. Ordinary trade and trust-based promises remain possible outside First Contract jurisdiction.

traits.name: Severed
traits.description: Your removed First Contract signature cannot be invoked for pact enforcement, signature-keyed detection, or Fraying. This is not universal magic immunity or invisibility. You lack pact preservation, eat, drink, sleep, and slowly age. Pact-dependent legal standing is lost; ordinary trade elsewhere remains possible.

effects.name: The Pact's Silence
effects.description: First Contract enforcement cannot invoke your removed signature. A Clause of Binding or Vezan cannot enforce that signature, but a creature can still see or physically attack you and unrelated magic works normally.
effects.mechanicsText: No First Contract signature enforcement or Fraying. No blanket advantage against spells or immunity to unrelated magic.

effects.name: Legal Non-Existence
effects.description: You are not a person under Athien law. Disadvantage on all social checks made with Athien, who cannot legally acknowledge your testimony, property claims, or contractual standing. and, you cannot benefit from Athien social institutions (inheritance, marriage, formal trade). Among the Riven and in the wider world, this carries no penalty, but in any Athien jurisdiction, you are a ghost.
effects.mechanicsText: You have disadvantage on social checks made with Athien, who cannot legally acknowledge your existence, testimony, or property.

effects.name: The Unpreserved Form
effects.description: You no longer benefit from the pact's preservation. You must eat, drink, and sleep normally. You age, slowly, but irreversibly. The silver in your skin will eventually dull to grey, and you will die of age in a way no other Athien ever has. No Riven has lived long enough yet to know how long that takes.

statusEffect.description: Must eat, drink, and sleep normally. Ages slowly but irreversibly. Will eventually die of old age.

effects.mechanicsText: Severed from the pact's preservation, you must eat, drink, and sleep normally, and you age slowly but irreversibly until you eventually die of old age.

traits.name: Silence-Walker
traits.description: Trained silence-walking grants advantage on Stealth checks. First Contract signature-keyed tracking cannot find your removed signature, but ordinary tracks, scent, eyes, and unrelated magical sensors can reveal you. Your voice has no pact-weight in First Contract courts.

effects.name: Beyond the Web
effects.description: Advantage on Stealth checks through trained movement. First Contract signature-keyed detection cannot invoke your removed name; ordinary tracks, scent, fungal senses, and unrelated magical tracking are not automatically defeated.
effects.mechanicsText: Advantage on Stealth checks. Detection resistance is limited to your removed First Contract signature; it is not universal untraceability.

effects.name: The Witnessed Absence
effects.description: You cannot give testimony in a Athien court. Your voice carries no pact-weight. Among the Athien, your words are legally meaningless, you cannot serve as a witness, sign a contract, or testify to anything. Among non-Athien, this carries no penalty, but among the pact-bound, you are a silence where a voice should be.

statusEffect.description: Cannot serve as witness, sign contracts, or provide legal testimony within Athien jurisdictions.

effects.mechanicsText: Within Athien jurisdictions you cannot serve as a witness, sign contracts, or provide legal testimony, as your voice carries no pact-weight.

traits.name: Bog-Hardened
traits.description: Resistance to blight damage and advantage on Survival checks in swamps, bogs, or the Bryngloom Forest. When you enter a location holding a strong First Contract copy (Atropolis, Ironjaw Port), you must make a DC 12 Constitution save or be sickened for 1 hour. (You survived the Severing and the bog that followed; the deep wild has stopped trying to kill you.)

effects.name: Deep Bog Endurance
effects.description: Resistance to blight damage. Advantage on Survival checks made in swamps, bogs, or the Bryngloom Forest. You have survived the Severing and the bog that followed, the deep wild is not your home, but it has stopped trying to kill you.
effects.mechanicsText: You have resistance to blight damage and advantage on Survival checks made in swamps, bogs, or the Bryngloom Forest.

effects.name: The Pact-Sickness
effects.description: When you enter a location with a strong copy of the First Contract (Atropolis, Ironjaw Port), you must make a DC 12 Constitution saving throw. On a failure, you are sickened for 1 hour, nausea, headache, a sense of being watched by something that cannot quite see you. The pact's presence is physically uncomfortable to a severed Athien, like a sound just below hearing, like a light just beyond vision. You can push through, but you will not enjoy it.

statusEffect.description: DC 12 CON save when near strong First Contract copies. Failure: sickened for 1 hour.

effects.mechanicsText: When you enter a location holding a strong First Contract copy (Atropolis, Ironjaw Port), you must make a DC 12 Constitution save or be sickened for 1 hour.

traits.name: Null-Strike
traits.description: Once per short rest, make a melee attack that deals +1d4 arcane damage. On hit, dispel one magical effect currently active on the target (GM chooses if multiple). Your severed nature unravels magic on contact; the pact cannot feel you, and neither can its spells.

effects.name: Severed Edge
effects.description: Make a melee attack. On hit, the attack deals +1d4 arcane damage. Your severed nature unravels magic on contact.

statusEffect.description: Melee attack deals +1d4 arcane damage on hit.

effects.mechanicsText: On a hit, your melee attack deals an additional +1d4 arcane damage.

effects.name: The Unraveling Touch
effects.description: On a hit, dispel one magical effect currently active on the target. If multiple magical effects are active, the GM chooses which is dispelled. The pact cannot feel you, and neither can its spells.

statusEffect.description: On hit, dispel one magical effect on the target (GM chooses if multiple).

effects.mechanicsText: On a hit, dispel one magical effect currently active on the target (the GM chooses if multiple are present).

vreken.name: Mycellan
vreken.illustrationCaption: “We guard the memory of what was drowned; in the darkness of the mire, only the patient eye perceives the path.” — Crypt-Scholar of the Sunken Spire
vreken.cardFlavor: Amber-eyed crypt-keepers who tend the Sunken Spire reverse cathedrals beneath the Bryngloom bogs.
vreken.visualDescription: Compact and wiry, standing 4'10" to 5'6", with long tapered ears that gracefully curl upward like spiral horns rising from beneath dark cowl hoods. Their eyes are bioluminescent lantern-eyes peeking from beneath the hood, glowing with rust-amber (Bedel Deep-Glow) or silver-white (Cromyx Ghost-Mycelium) light in the dark. Their lower faces are wrapped in cloth, and their long-fingered hands are built for delicate spore-harvesting. They wear gothic monastic vestments in dark earth tones with gold-woven trim, living in inverted reverse cathedral-monasteries (Sunken Spires) carved into peat-stone.
vreken.description:
**[The Lantern-Eyed Crypt-Speakers]**, *Leaning into the damp peat-stone of the Sunken Spire, a Mycellan keeper with upward-curling horn-ears and glowing rust-amber eyes traces a fingertip along glowing fungal filaments in an inverted catacomb.*

The Ghost-Mycelium (the volatile, glowing fungal strain that the Cromyx carry) is Morvane's wounded nervous system made visible. It glows because Morvane is in pain. The Mycellan bonded with it not by choice but because it grew into them the way a disease grows into a population that cannot leave. Their lantern-eyes are the visible cost of a devotion they cannot renounce, and their greatest tragedy, the Over-Lit, the ones who chased the fungal-hush too far and burned out from within, is not a flaw in the design; it is the cost of living with a light that was never meant to be theirs.
quickFacts: Once an elegant elven people devoted to Morvane, the ancient bog-deity of decay. When the Wyrd wounded their god, the fungal networks they cultivated turned invasive, threading through their nervous systems, curling their ears, lighting their eyes, and transforming them into compact, wiry crypt-keepers the surface world calls goblin-like.

Their lantern-eyes glow with bioluminescence, rust-amber for the stable Bedel bloodline, silver-white for the volatile Cromyx. The Cromyx carry Ghost-Mycelium, Morvane's wounded nerve-tissue made symbiotic, granting extraordinary perception at the cost of vulnerability to the hush: an intoxicating, addictive fungal euphoria that hollows out those who chase it too far.

Play a Mycellan to carry a wound you did not choose from a god you cannot leave. Your people were the Gloom's first children, but newcomers profited from your suffering deity while you paid in flesh. The Root-Veil is failing, the Cromyx are rising up, and if Morvane dies, the Athien's immortality dies with it.
vreken.culturalBackground:
Mycellan culture is monastic, alternative, and deeply rooted in their bond with the wounded land. Two institutions shape every aspect of their society: the crypt and the spore.

The crypt is their social institution. Mycellan do not bury their dead in earth. They entomb them in inverted cathedrals carved into the Gloom's peat-stone, vaulted chambers lit only by the fungal shrouds of ancestors whose bodies still emit light generations after death. The Sunken Spires descend into the earth rather than rising toward the sky, their spires pointing downward into the dark peat-stone, each spiraling gallery older and deeper than the last. A family's status is measured by how many generations their crypt still glows. Wealth is measured in ancestral light. Every Mycellan cathedral is also a mausoleum, the walls lined with preserved dead whose fungal wrappings continue to emit the lantern-glow of their bloodline. Priests, called Veil-Speakers, sing the names of the crypt's dead in endless rotation, so that no light is ever truly extinguished.

The spore is their sustenance and their craft. The Mycellan cultivate phosphorescent fungi in their crypt-cathedrals for food, medicine, light, and ritual purposes. Spore-gardens line the lower galleries of every Sunken Spire, tended by keepers who can read a fungal bloom's health by the color of its glow. They are stealthy, centuries of navigating the dark, dangerous Bryngloom have made them masters of concealment, and their approach to problems is unconventional: where other races meet obstacles with force or negotiation, the Mycellan circumvent, subvert, or simply wait until the obstacle decomposes.

The Over-Lit are the wound in Mycellan society. The phosphorescent fungi the Mycellan cultivate are not merely a resource, they are intoxicating. Prolonged exposure to concentrated fungal glow induces a euphoric, sedative state called "the hush." In moderation, the ambient light of caverns and crypts is harmless, even meditative. But concentrated doses, raw fungal pulp pressed against the skin, inhaled spore-vapor, direct ingestion, produce a deeper, addictive high. The Over-Lit are Mycellan who chased the hush too far. Their lantern-eyes burn bright at all times, they can no longer dim them. Their bodies grow gaunt, their movements twitchy, their skin pale and translucent as the glow eats through them from within. They cluster in shanties at the edges of settlements, tolerated, pitied, feared. Every Mycellan knows someone who fell. Every Cromyx, those of the Ghost-Mycelium bloodline, whose sensitivity makes them uniquely vulnerable, worries it could be them.

The Inquisitors are the Mycellan who hunt their own. When an Over-Lit progresses beyond recovery, when the hush has hollowed them out completely and they have become a danger to others, the Inquisitors are called. They are Cromyx who have trained themselves to track their own kind through the deep caves by spore-sign and sound. They are feared, respected, and deeply isolated. To kill a kinsman, even one already lost to the hush, is a burden that no Bedel, those of the Deep-Glow bloodline, less vulnerable to the hush, can truly understand.

Mycellan architecture is gothic monastic: low, arched stone halls built around central crypt-courtyards where ancestral light provides the only illumination. Vaulted ceilings. Narrow lancet windows that admit no outside light, the interior glows from within. Settlements are organized like abbeys: chapter house, infirmary, scriptorium, crypt. Every structure descends rather than rises, the spires of a Mycellan cathedral reach into the earth, not toward the sky. Their most sacred spaces are the deepest, closest to the Root-Veil: the mycelial network beneath the Gloom that the Mycellan believe is Morvane's wounded nervous system, the conduit through which their deity still, faintly, lives.

The Athien and the Mycellan share the Bryngloom Forest and barely speak. The Athien arrived centuries after the corruption began, a frail dying people fleeing the surface freeze who made their own desperate bargain with the same Morvane whose suffering had already transformed the Mycellan, and profited from it. The Athien got pale skin and immortality. The Mycellan, who had been suffering for centuries, got nothing. The Athien view the Mycellan as archaic victims, a people who surround themselves with glowing dead relatives when they could be running a trade empire. The Mycellan view the Athien as spiritual parasites, profiting from the same deity whose wound still bleeds through Mycellan veins. Their relationship is coldly functional: trade routes, shared borders, fungal-light exports to Athien grave-cities in exchange for bog-preserved goods and cold-iron tools. Neither defers to the other. Neither particularly wants to.

The Solari of Sundale are the Mycellan's silent kindred. The Sol's Breath, the eternal ember the Solari tend, and the Root-Veil the Mycellan venerate emerged from the same era: the memory of warmth in a world that froze. Solari forge-pilgrims occasionally journey to Mycellan crypt-cathedrals. Mycellan spire-tenders occasionally travel to Sundale to trade cultivation techniques. Neither race speaks openly of what they recognize in each other. The recognition is enough.

To the humans of the surrounding regions, the Mycellan are the grave-lights: lantern-eyed keepers who live in upside-down cathedrals and sing to their dead. Their spore-craft is the finest in the known world. Their medicines work where others fail. But being treated by a Mycellan means lying on a stone slab in a mausoleum, ancestors glowing softly from every wall, while someone with too many joints and silver-glowing eyes tends a poultice of something that is still, faintly, alive. It works. It is unsettling. And the humans come anyway, because the alternative is worse. The Morren, the Bryngloom's old human population, once walked the same bogs; the blight of their bargain absorbed them into the Mycellan, and the debt they carried survives in the Mycellan's contracts to this day.
vreken.variantDiversity: The Mycellan are divided into two bloodlines, defined not by geography or ideology but by the fungal strain that grew into their ancestors when the Wyrd wounded Morvane. The Bedel carry Deep-Glow, the oldest, most stable strain, less deeply threaded through the nervous system, granting immunity to the hush but dimmer lantern-eyes. The Cromyx carry Ghost-Mycelium, Morvane's wounded nerve-tissue made symbiotic, volatile and brilliant, granting extraordinary perception at the cost of addiction and stigma. The Over-Lit are not a third bloodline. They are Cromyx who fell.

integrationNotes.actionPointSystem: Mycellan abilities focus on perception, spore-craft, healing, and the fungal bond. Their lantern-eyes provide bioluminescence but make stealth difficult in darkness.
integrationNotes.backgroundSynergy: Mycellan excel in backgrounds emphasizing medicine, nature, and survival. Their crypt-culture creates compelling roleplay opportunities around devotion, legacy, and the Over-Lit epidemic.
integrationNotes.classCompatibility: The Bedel are native to the Animist (channel ancestral spirits through the forest's fungal memory), the Plaguebringer (Vespera's own branch), and the Revenant (Kora's covenant). The Cromyx are native to the Inquisitor (hunt your own corrupted kin through the mycelial network), the Plaguebringer (seed it across miles of root), the Apex (mycelium-scent), and the Augur (root-mushroom pulses). No other people is native to these paths.

vreken.diasporaVariation: Mycellan diaspora is sparse but old, lantern-eyed crypt-keepers serve as spore-cultivators, healers, and ancestral-consultants in every region's burial grounds. A Nordhalla-Mycellan (serving the Frozen Archive's glacier-tombs) has adapted to the cold their southern kin cannot bear, their bioluminescence dimmed to a faint blue that the glacier-ice amplifies. A Sundale-Mycellan is rare and grim, the volcanic heat distresses their fungal-bonded skin, and they cluster in the deep ash-tombs beneath the Ashen Escarpment. The Bryngloom remains the only region with a large Mycellan population; elsewhere they are solitary practitioners, respected, avoided, and slowly losing their Root-Veil connection the further they roam from the wounded land that made them.
vreken.meaningfulTradeoffs: Mycellan gain unparalleled perception of the Root-Veil and the underground world through their fungal bond, but their bioluminescent eyes make stealth difficult and their tie to a wounded god carries a physical and emotional toll. The Cromyx live with the constant threat of the Over-Lit addiction.

baseTraits.build: Wiry and compact, long-fingered, curled ears, lantern-bioluminescent eyes

sharedTraits.name: Hush Vulnerability
sharedTraits.description: +25% vulnerability to blight damage from fungal sources. When exposed to concentrated Ghost-Mycelium spores for 1+ minute, make a DC 12 Constitution save or suffer disadvantage on Perception for 1 hour as the hush clouds your senses. Bedel bloodlines, whose deep-glow immunity purges fungal contamination, are exempt from this vulnerability.

effects.name: Hush Susceptibility
effects.description: +25% blight damage from fungal sources. DC 12 Constitution save on concentrated fungal exposure or disadvantage on Perception for 1 hour.
effects.mechanicsText: +25% blight damage from fungal sources; on 1+ min concentrated fungal spore exposure, DC 12 Constitution save or Perception disadvantage for 1 hour.

sharedTraits.name: Lantern-Eyes
sharedTraits.description: Your irises emit a faint, steady bioluminescence, rust-amber or silver-white depending on your bloodline, the visible sign of the fungal symbiosis forced on your ancestors when the Wyrd wounded Morvane. The glow illuminates your immediate surroundings with the same cold light your kin have cultivated in the crypt-cathedrals since the corruption began. But a light that guides is also a light that betrays: your eyes are visible in darkness from sixty feet away, and no shadow can fully hide them.

effects.name: The Betraying Light
effects.description: Your lantern-eyes are visible in darkness from up to 60 feet. Disadvantage on Stealth checks made in dim light or darkness, your own eyes illuminate you, and no hood or shadow can fully extinguish the glow.
effects.mechanicsText: Disadvantage on Stealth checks in dim light or darkness; lantern-eyes visible up to 60 ft.

sharedTraits.name: Spore-Sense
sharedTraits.description: Your fungal bond reads the living network of the Root-Veil. Generations of symbiosis with the wounded land have attuned you to the spore-signatures of fungal growth, underground currents, and the slow pulse of the bog. When in underground environments or areas of heavy fungal growth, you sense the health of the mycelial network around you and read the terrain as fluently as a surface-dweller reads a road.

effects.name: Spore-Sight
effects.description: Advantage on Nature and Survival checks made in underground environments or areas of heavy fungal growth. You read the health of the mycelial network and the terrain it threads through.
effects.mechanicsText: Advantage on Nature and Survival checks in underground environments or areas of heavy fungal growth.

vreken.epicHistory:
The Mycellan are the Bryngloom Forest's oldest living memory, and they were not always what they are.

Before the sun died, before the Athien wrote their first contract in bog-iron ink, before the Noble Families drew their borders and sealed their bargains, the Mycellan were already here, an elven people, contemplative and monastic, devoted to Morvane, the ancient bog-deity who governed the threshold between life and decay. They built their cathedral-monasteries deep in the earth, beneath the peat-bogs, singing to Morvane in the fungal-lit dark. They were elegant, peaceful, and old. Their spires pointed downward into the peat-stone, their vaulted crypt-chambers lit by the ancestral fungal-glow they had cultivated for millennia. The Root-Veil (the mycelial network beneath the forest, Morvane's nervous system) was their communion, the medium through which they spoke to their deity and their deity spoke back.

Then the Wyrd came. When Sol was bound and the surface world froze, the corruption seeped up through the roots of the Bryngloom. Morvane was wounded, not killed, but poisoned, its domain of patient decay turned malignant by Keth Amar's spreading influence. The Root-Veil, the conduit that connected the Mycellan to their deity, became a conduit for the poison. The Mycellan did not fall all at once. The corruption took generations. The fungal networks they had cultivated turned invasive, threading through their nervous systems. Their ears, once elegantly pointed, began to curl inward at the tips. Their eyes (once elven, dark, and clear) developed the bioluminescent fungal growths that would become their lantern-eyes. Their elegant forms devolved: still graceful in vestige, still elven in bone-structure, but changed. Cromyx. Wrong, by the standards of a world that had never seen what they were before. They did not choose this. They did not bargain for it. They were tied to a wounded god, and when the god was poisoned, the poison flowed downhill into everything connected to it.

The Athien arrived three centuries after the Great Binding, a frail, dying people fleeing the surface freeze. They walked into the deep wood where Morvane waited (the same Morvane whose suffering had already transformed the Mycellan) and presented a case. You are the record-keeper of the forest. We are the record-keepers of civilization. If we die, the record dies. If you preserve us, we will record everything. Morvane accepted. Not from compassion, from pragmatism. The Athien rose from the bog with pale skin and stilled breath, and the First Contract appeared in the heartwood of the oldest ironwood tree. The Mycellan, who had been suffering for centuries, watched newcomers profit from the same deity that had cursed them, and said nothing. Two intelligent species sharing a forest, one ancient and wounded, one newborn and preserved. The relationship has been coldly functional ever since.

The Over-Lit epidemic began in the fifth century after the Great Binding. With the Athien's trade networks bringing surface goods into the Gloom for the first time, Mycellan fungal exports became valuable currency. Harvest intensified. Exposure intensified. The first recorded case of the hush, a Cromyx Veil-Speaker named Aedris who pressed raw Ghost-Mycelium pulp to her eyes during a prolonged crypt-vigil and was found three days later, still glowing, still singing, but no longer able to recognize her own reflection, sent a tremor through Mycellan society that has never fully settled. The Inquisition was founded within a decade of the first recorded Over-Lit case. The Bedel began their drift toward leadership positions during the sixth century, their biological stability translating into political dominance.

The Mycellan have never had a war. They have never had a king. They have never been conquered. The Bryngloom Forest is too deep, too dark, too labyrinthine for any surface army to navigate, and the Mycellan themselves are too distributed, too entrenched in their crypt-cathedrals, too difficult to find. They are the only race in the Ethnologue that has survived without violence, without imperialism, without a great leader or a unifying crisis, though they carry a wound older than any war. Their history is not a record of battles. It is a record of light, who glowed, who dimmed, who over-lit, and who is still burning, waiting for the day Morvane heals or the day the corruption finally finishes what it began.

notableFigures.name: Aedris the First-Lit
notableFigures.title: The Warning
notableFigures.backstory:
The first recorded Over-Lit and the reason the Inquisition exists. Aedris was a Cromyx Veil-Speaker of extraordinary devotion, her silver-white lantern-eyes burning with the Ghost-Mycelium strain that is Morvane's wounded nerve-tissue made visible. For forty years she served as the crypt-speaker of the Sunken Spire, the oldest Mycellan cathedral in the Gloom, singing the names of seventeen generations of entombed ancestors and tending the fungal shrouds that kept the dead glowing. She believed, with the fervor only the deeply faithful possess, that the Root-Veil could still carry Morvane's true voice beneath the pain of the wound.

During a prolonged crypt-vigil, a traditional ritual where a Veil-Speaker remains in the deepest crypt-chamber for seven days without surfacing, maintaining the ancestral chant alone and communing with the Root-Veil, Aedris pressed raw Ghost-Mycelium pulp to her eyes to keep herself awake. She believed the deeper communion would let her hear Morvane speak. The hush took her on the third day. When the other Veil-Speakers descended to relieve her, they found her still singing, still glowing, but her eyes had burned so bright they had bleached the crypt-stone around her to pale grey. She could not recognize her own reflection. She kept asking why a stranger was standing in her cathedral.

Aedris lived for another eleven years before the hush completed its hollowing. During that time she was studied, pitied, and carefully avoided. Her final words, recorded by the Veil-Speaker who witnessed her death, were: "Morvane is still singing. I just cannot remember the words." The Inquisition was founded within the decade. Her crypt, in the deepest chamber of the Sunken Spire, still emits a faint silver glow that no other lantern has ever been able to match.

notableFigures.name: Orven the Still-Handed
notableFigures.title: The First Inquisitor
notableFigures.backstory:
The founder of the Inquisition and the most feared Mycellan in history, not by outsiders, but by his own people. Orven was a Cromyx whose twin sister, Seris, over-lit when they were both forty-three. The hush hollowed her over the course of a year. By the end, she had become a danger, her lantern-light blinding, her hunger for the hush overriding every other instinct. She had attacked three other Mycellan trying to steal their fungal stores. The crypt-council debated for a week. Orven did not wait for their decision.

He tracked his sister through the Gloom's deepest caves for four days, following the spore-sign she left behind and the sound of her burning glow echoing off the cavern walls. He found her in a dead-end cavern, surrounded by the empty husks of fungal blooms she had consumed, her eyes burning so brightly they cast her own shadow against the far wall. She recognized him. She asked him to stay. He did what he had come to do.

Orven spent the following decades training other Cromyx to do what he had done: find the Over-Lit who had progressed beyond recovery and end them before they could harm others. He never married. He never spoke more than was necessary. The Inquisitors still follow the protocol he established: the kill must be witnessed by at least two other Inquisitors, the name of the Over-Lit must be added to the crypt-singing as a warning, and the body must be returned to a Sunken Spire for proper entombment. Orven's own name is sung first, every rotation, before all the others. In his later years, he descended deeper into the Bryngloom than any Inquisitor before him, following the Root-Veil toward its wounded source. He stopped reporting back. He is not confirmed dead. The Inquisitors wait for word that may never come.

notableFigures.name: Isara Deep-Glow
notableFigures.title: The Matriarch of the Bedel
notableFigures.backstory:
The Mycellan who first articulated what the Bedel had always quietly believed: that their less-severe transformation was not luck but a sign of being less entangled in Morvane's wound, and that this carried a duty. Isara was born nine generations after Aedris over-lit, into a Bedel bloodline that had never produced a single case of the hush. She was educated in the scriptoriums, learned the crypt-records, and noticed a pattern that no one else had wanted to see: the Bedel were not more virtuous. They were less touched. Their Deep-Glow strain had threaded less deeply through their nervous systems, left their features closer to the old elven forms, left their minds more stable, and that stability had, over generations, silently translated into leadership, into trade delegations, into council seats, into a quiet assumption that the Bedel were the face the Mycellan should show to the world.

Isara did not invent this inequality. She named it. In a series of scriptorium essays, the closest thing the Mycellan have to political theory, she argued that the Bedel had a duty to lead, not out of superiority but out of stability: the Cromyx were too volatile, too vulnerable, too deeply entangled in the wounded Root-Veil to be trusted with continuity. The Bedel had an obligation to ensure the monasteries endured. The essays became the unofficial justification for the social hierarchy that already existed.

The Cromyx have never forgiven her. The Bedel have never stopped citing her. Isara herself, according to the crypt-records, spent her final years in the Sunken Spire's deepest chamber, tending Aedris's eternal silver glow, and writing nothing at all.

majorLocations.name: The Sunken Spire
majorLocations.description: Carved radially into the deep bogs of the Bryngloom, **The Sunken Spire** represents the spiritual heart of Mycellan civilization. An inverted gothic cathedral built into a natural four-hundred-foot sinkhole, its spire points downward into the dark earth, its nave spiraling along the peat-stone walls down to the sanctuary, where the Veil-Speakers sing the names of the glowing dead in tattered fungal shrouds. The deeper chambers house the crypt of Aedris the First-Lit, whose eternal pale-moonlight glow is tended in six-hour shifts by silent priests practicing the Vault-Breath. The Mycellan share the Bryngloom with the Athien, whose canopy-city **Atropolis** dominates the upper canopy; the Mycellan hold the deep bog below.

majorLocations.name: The Hollow-Scriptorium
majorLocations.description: The intellectual center of the Bryngloom Forest, where Mycellan Inscriptors carve historical genealogies and spore-lore onto compressed fungal-wood tablets using glowing Ghost-Mycelium stylus-points. It is heavily controlled by the **Bedel**, who enforce strict access regulations on the heretical or volatile Cromyx scholars, restricting them from reading the oldest ancestral archives.

majorLocations.name: The Over-Shanty
majorLocations.description: At the edges of every cathedral-complex sits the Over-Shanty, a squalid shantytown of the **Over-Lit**, those Cromyx whose lantern-eyes have been burned past dimming by spore-addiction (the hush). The shanties are a constant reminder of the physical and psychological toll of Mycellan biology, heavily patrolled by the Inquisition who monitor kinsmen for the final hollowing.

vreken.currentCrisis: The central crisis is the deepening of Morvane's wound, and the fear that the Root-Veil's slow failure will accelerate the Mycellan's devolution past any hope of recovery. The **Ghost-Mycelium** grows brighter and more volatile each generation, the Cromyx read this as Morvane's pain worsening, the Bedel read it as the corruption spreading. The **Cromyx** have begun the **Bright-Speaking**, a heretical movement demanding scriptorium access and an end to the Bedel's monopoly on leadership, arguing that those who feel Morvane's wound most closely should be the ones tending the cure. Tensions are peaking as a Cromyx coven prepares to force entry into the deepest galleries of the Hollow-Scriptorium to find records of a failed rite that some believe could cleanse the Root-Veil, while Athien merchants watch the instability, preparing to exploit any slip in the fungal-light trade, and quietly aware that if Morvane dies, their own First Contract dies with it.
vreken.culturalPractices:
Every Mycellan child learns the crypt-chant before they learn to read fungal-wood script. The first lesson, taught at the age when a human child would be learning to walk, is "the bog remembers."
